title: Route tables, internet gateway and NAT gateway

videos.script: Lesson sixteen left the shop with nine subnets and no way out. {{nine}} This lesson gives them one, and every way out is a line in a route table. {{table}} A route table is a list of destinations, each with a target. Every subnet uses exactly one. When a packet leaves a machine, the table of its subnet decides where it goes. {{igw}} The first target is an internet gateway, the VPC's door to the internet. One route to it, for every address, and three subnets become public. {{nat}} The other six must not be reachable from outside, but they still need to call out. For them there is the NAT gateway. It sits in a public subnet and opens connections in one direction only. {{prefix}} When several routes match a packet, the most specific one wins. You will read three packets through a table and see where each one lands. {{zones}} Then comes the bill. A NAT gateway belongs to one zone and is charged by the hour. One per zone costs three times as much. One for all turns a zone's failure into everybody's. {{end}} By the end you can read any route table and say where a packet goes, and what the way out costs.
